cim_eredeti: Part I: Tackling Informal Economy With Artificial Intelligence
szoveg_eredeti:
Pakistan cannot broaden its tax base by repeatedly squeezing people already visible to the State. Artificial intelligence offers a different route: build a national economic registry that can distinguish taxable capacity from dependency, lawful informality from criminal activity, and taxpayers from those entitled to social protection

Pakistan’s tax debate begins with the wrong number. Every year governments ask how many income-tax returns have been filed. They celebrate another increase with no meaning rise in tax paid with returns, announce a fresh documentation drive and then return authorised too the same narrow circle of salaried persons, incorporated businesses, importers, bank depositors and consumers already visible to the State.

By October 14, 2026, the Federal Board of Revenue (FBR) had received 6.71 million income-tax returns, up 34.38% over the comparable period last year but tax paid was lower than last time. The improvement in number is, thus, ceremonial. It also exposes the scale of the problem of voluntary compliance and tax avoidance and evasion in Pakistan.

Pakistan live population at worldometers (accessed at 10am on October 23, 2026) was 260.5 million, out of which, working-age/adult-group (15–60 years) is roughly 180 million, but active labour force officially is about 95 million. However, labour force data is highly controversial due to huge size of informal economy and correct reporting as well as faulty mythology [Aneel & Muneeb, Islamabad Policy Research Institute, October 2025].

Artificial Intelligence And The Future Of The International Order: Competing Visions From America

Pakistan's total informal labour force is estimated at approximately 65.4 million to 70+ million workers, based on a national labor force of around 95 million and an informal sector share of roughly 76% to 80% (State Bank series, Gallup Pakistan and PIDE). Amongst all in formal and informal sector about 30 million earn taxable income (both agricultural and non-agricultural), yet only a fraction appears meaningfully inside the direct-tax system at FBR and provincial agencies authorise to collect agricultural income tax.1

Artificial Intelligence And The Future Of Stock Markets: Enhancing Efficiency Or Amplifying Risk?

The explanation is not simply tax evasion. Pakistan Bureau of Statistics (PBS) places informal-sector employment at 72.5% of non-agricultural employment. In rural areas the share is 76.2%; even urban Pakistan records 68.5%. The latest Labour Force Survey also shows that own-account workers form a very large share of the informal sector. Pakistan is, in economic terms, overwhelmingly informal.2

That informality contains very different worlds. A home-based seamstress paid in cash is informal. So is a mechanic without registration, a street vendor, a carpenter, a small family shop, a freelance technician and millions of self-employed workers. Their economic activity may be completely lawful although the State cannot adequately observe their incomes, assets, family dependency or eligibility for social protection.

At the other end lie kidnapping for ransom, smuggling, narcotics, bhatta (extortion), counterfeit trade, illegal currency movement, trade-based money laundering, proceeds of corruption etc. and organised crime. These two economies must never be confused.

Our work beginning with Pakistan: From Hash to Heroin and its sequel Pakistan: From Drug-trap to Debt-trap documented how narcotics, weapons, informal finance, smuggling and political protection created parallel circuits of wealth. That criminal economy does not need ordinary formalisation. It requires detection, confiscation, prosecution and disruption.

Pakistan At 79: Artificial Intelligence, Digital Finance And The Future Of National Innovation

The lawful informal economy needs something entirely different: visibility without harassment. This distinction has largely disappeared from tax policy.

FBR’s habitual response has been to tax whatever it can already see. Withholding taxes on banking transactions/profits, electricity, telecommunications, imports, contracts, property and numerous other transactions collect income tax before real income has even been determined. The documented economy therefore carries an increasingly heavy compliance burden while substantial actual income remains outside assessment.

Our 2024 PRIME study, Towards Broad, Flat, Low-rate and Predictable Taxes, argues that Pakistan’s wider economic tax base is around Rs. 500 trillion after taking the informal economy into account. It estimated around 30 million persons with taxable income above Rs. 600,000 and showed how a broad base combined with low rates and credible enforcement could yield revenue far beyond present collections. The precise numbers must now be updated, but the basic point remains: Pakistan’s revenue problem is not absence of economic activity; it is failure to identify it fairly and systematically.3

Is Artificial Intelligence Gaining Consciousness Or Going Rogue?

It is to make the State capable of knowing which citizens can fairly contribute, which businesses should be brought into the mainstream, which economic activity is criminal—and which households should instead receive protection. That is the difference between surveillance and economic intelligence

Artificial intelligence (AI) creates an opportunity to reverse this model. Anthony Tan’s recent Finance & Development article for the International Monetary Fund (IMF) makes the central point well: AI policy in developing economies must be designed around the lives people actually lead, not around an assumption that everyone is a salaried worker with a formal employer, bank account and complete digital trail.4

Pakistan already possesses much of the identity infrastructure required for a different approach. By the end of fiscal year (FY) 2025-26 the country had roughly 164 million broadband connections, about 159.5 million of them mobile.

Telecom subscriptions crossed 210 million on August 31, 2026. Mobile SIMs are biometrically linked, while CNICs connect individuals to NADRA. Banks, property registries, vehicle records, utilities, employers, customs systems and social-protection programmes each hold fragments of economic information.5

Foundations First: Why Artificial Intelligence Cannot Solve Pakistan’s Primary Education Crisis

The problem is that the State sees fragments rather than economic relationships. The answer should be a National Economic Registry, separate in purpose from a conventional tax roll.

Every adult biometric mobile user could be asked through a text message, a secure mobile or web interface, a few simple questions: Are you economically dependent? If yes, upon whom? Are you employed? If yes, identify the employer. Are you self-employed? If yes, state the profession, trade or business and, where available, its registration or tax number. Are you an employer or business owner? Are you unemployed, retired, studying or otherwise outside the labour force?

No tax should arise merely from answering these questions. The first purpose is classification, not assessment. The responses could then be matched, under strict statutory safeguards, with existing government datasets.

AI can identify inconsistencies: a person declaring complete dependency while holding several high-value assets; an unregistered business receiving substantial commercial payments; an employer paying dozens of workers who do not appear in payroll declarations; or a household receiving social assistance despite economic indicators inconsistent with eligibility.

Islamic Heritage in the Age of Artificial Intelligence: Preserving Values, Shaping The Future
